summary: Jesus contrasts a Pharisee who prayed about his own goodness with a tax collector who begged for mercy, and says the tax collector went home justified.
key_insight: The Pharisee “prayed thus with himself.” In two sentences he says “I” five times and asks God for nothing. The tax collector asks for one thing, mercy, and he is the one who goes home justified.
story: Jesus told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others.
“Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.”

The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself: “God, I thank You that I am not like other men.” He named the extortioners, the unjust and the adulterers, “or even as this tax collector.” Then he listed his record: “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess.”
The tax collector stood far off. He would not so much as raise his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, “God, be merciful to me a sinner!”
“I tell you,” Jesus said, “this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

scene.label: Prayer in the temple
scene.text: Public prayers were offered in the temple at the morning and afternoon sacrifices, and people came to pray at other hours as well (compare Acts 3:1). Standing was the normal posture for prayer.

scene.label: Beyond the Law
scene.text: The Law required one fast a year; devout Pharisees fasted twice a week, by later custom on Mondays and Thursdays. The Law required tithes of grain, wine, oil, herds and flocks (Leviticus 27:30–32; Deuteronomy 14:22–23); this man tithed everything he acquired. By the standards of his day, he was an exceptionally religious man.

scene.label: Standing afar off
scene.text: The tax collector kept his distance and his eyes down. Beating the breast was a sign of grief and shame; Luke uses the same picture of the crowds leaving the cross (Luke 23:48).

scene.label: “Be merciful”
scene.text: The tax collector’s word for “be merciful” is related to atonement. The same root appears where Hebrews says Christ came “to make propitiation for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 2:17). In Greek he calls himself the sinner, as if there were no other.

scene.label: Justified
scene.text: To be justified is to be declared right with God. Paul builds on this word when he writes of the God “who justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5).

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records this parable, and he names its audience: those who trusted in themselves and despised others. He sets it beside the persistent widow, so two parables on prayer stand together, one about not giving up and one about the heart that prays. Next Luke tells of infants brought to Jesus, who bring nothing and receive the kingdom.

seeing.reveals: Jesus pronounces heaven’s verdict on two worshipers. The man God accepts is the one who brought nothing but his sin and a plea for mercy.
seeing.living: It is possible to pray in the temple and still be talking to yourself. Come to God as the tax collector did, with no comparisons and no list, and trust Him to justify. And watch for the quiet contempt that measures you against “this tax collector.”
seeing.ponder: Whom do you quietly thank God you are not like? What would it sound like to pray only, “God, be merciful to me a sinner”?

preaching.big_idea: God sends home justified not those who list their virtues, but those who plead for mercy.
outline: A prayer that looked in the mirror (11–12)
A prayer that looked for mercy (13)
preaching.watch_for: Both men “went up” to the temple; only one “went down to his house justified” (vv. 10, 14). The closing proverb also ends Jesus’ teaching on places at the wedding feast (Luke 14:11).
